newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: China seen flexing muscles in Australia row.
newsitem.headline: China seen flexing muscles in Australia row.

text.p: China's anger over the warm Australian welcome for the Dalai Lama was fanned by nationalism and domestic politics, posing no real threat to bilateral trade and political relations, analysts said on Wednesday.

As Australian politicians played down the rift, analysts said the row highlighted Beijing's increasingly assertive foreign policy as it prepared for a more prominent international role in the new century.

"There is a certain bluntness about Chinese diplomacy these days which underlines the growing self-confidence of a nation that believes it is headed for bigger and better things," wrote Sydney Morning Herald commentator Stephen Hutcheon.

China expert Professor Ian Wilson told Reuters that Beijing's hostility to the decision by Prime Minister John Howard to meet the exiled Tibetan spiritual leader was guided more by growing nationalism and uncertainty about the leadership succession in China than any real anger with Howard's conservative government.
"We are in for the great Chinese curse of living in interesting times," the Australian National University professor said.
As the importance of hardline communism faded in the world's most populous country, nationalism was taking on an increasingly important role, he said.
And despite the likelihood that President Jiang Zemin would eventually succeed paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, uncertainty over the succession continued in Beijing, he said.

Wilson said Beijing, having issued strong public warnings against Howard meeting the Tibetan Buddhist leader, was now bound to carry out its threatened retaliation to reinforce its position on the man they see as a trouble-maker pushing for independence for his Himalayan homeland.
The Dalai Lama has urged Howard to press Beijing to open negotiations on autonomy for Tibet.
"They might feel they have to make an object lesson of someone," he said.
"I think both polical and trade relations will cool considerably for a short term, but I don't think it's a long-term thing," he said.
Howard said on Wednesday that he would not bow to threats of trade retaliation from foreign governments.
"I hope they don't carry through with that threat, but I don't bow to threats," Howard said in a television interview.
On Tuesday, Beijing warned that any meeting with the Dalai Lama would harm economic and diplomatic ties between China and Australia.
The head of politics at the Australian Defence Force Academy in Canberra, Carl Thayer, told Reuters that Beijing was going through the motions in threatening retaliation.
"China is compelled to continue to make huffs and puffs," Thayer said. "It's Chinese opera, it's gongs and smoke and firecrackers.

"The Dalai Lama is not going to affect bilateral relations in any meaningful way if he is only received by Howard as a religious leader, and if Howard doesn't make any provocative statements," he said.

Howard's aides have stressed that the meeting, to be held on Thursday in the prime minister's Sydney office, is unofficial and that the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize winner was being seen as a religious leader.

Thayer, Wilson and other analysts also said China was concerned by new security pacts in the region, which it saw as an effort by foreign powers to contain it, including recent defence agreements between Canberra and Washington and Canberra and Jakarta.
